newsitem.title: UK: Metals Outlook - Markets set for daily stock repor.
newsitem.headline: Metals Outlook - Markets set for daily stock repor.

text.p: The London Metal Exchange (LME) started daily reporting of warehouse stock movements on Monday, which may over time reduce market price volatility, traders said.
Initially, interest will focus on whether the run of drawdowns of copper from Singapore to China continue or if much-talked of Chinese zinc arrives in the same destination.
The latest LME figures on Monday showed zinc stocks up by 5,000 tonnes, with 6,000 going into Singapore and 1,000 leaving Europe.
But eventually when the system beds down the market will be paying less attention.
"It will get to be so routine that people will just ignore it, as they do with Comex," one leading trader said.
Previously, inventory movements were reported by the LME twice-weekly, but as a consequence of the 1996 SIB review of the markets, the Exchange is moving towards greater transparency.
At some stage the LME may be in a position to say that tonnages of metal over a particular percentage are held by one quarter, but without divulging the identity.
However, some market sources were unsure if daily reporting was a measure that the LME really needed, given the reliability of its current data.
"It strikes me that this is a knee-jerk reaction by the LME - they had to be seen to be doing something," one analyst said.
Having to make inventory returns daily could put unnecessary pressure on some of the warehouse companies who may not be geared up to provide figures to the LME by a given time every day.
"It may end up that the LME will have to revise figures from time to time - that rarely happens now," he noted.
"This means more work for the warehouse companies. That is what extra rules and regulations do - they create work and add costs," another trader said.
Meanwhile, LME traders will also be looking to see how yen-based aluminium futures, which started trading on Japan's Tokyo Commodity Exchange (TOCOM) today, fare.
"This is really weird, as the TOCOM is very different from the LME, and as far as I can see they will only be interested in small speculators," a trader here said.
The local Japanese industry is opposed to the contract, so trade involvement will be minimal, with pricing remaining LME-based.
"But if some end-users do use it as a pricing medium, then the trade could be forced to use it," he said.
